deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations. It is a heavily corrected Latin draft of the theses (Theses) that Riemann was to defend at the public disputation for his doctorate on 16 Dec 1851. The next page shows drafts of the title page with that date. The theses refer to his Inaugural dissertation 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'.

The German header reads: 'The first point concerns the definition of a function of a variable complex quantity.'

The Latin preamble says, roughly: we did not write the preceding dissertation in a polemical manner, 'to use that word'. So that it may also furnish matter for the public disputation, we note the following propositions on which well-known authors, illustrious by the fame of their names, hold contrary opinions.

Thesis I concerns the definition of a function of a complex variable given in the dissertation (cited as p. 16). Only the opening words of the German quotation are copied: 'eine veränderliche Grösse, welche allgemein zu reden ...'.

Thesis II concerns a theorem stated in the dissertation (p. 16, art. 4 or 12; the reading is uncertain). It begins 'Wenn eine Function w von z ...'. The draft sets it against the opinion of 'ill. Cauchy', who has said something in several places; the rest is struck out.

Thesis III concerns the determination of a function of a complex variable. The methods usually used all start from an analytic expression, by means of which the value of the function is given for every determinate value of the argument. Previous authors who touched on this either:
- do not attribute to the function the notion that Riemann used for its definition; or
- hold that it does not belong to the definition (Cauchy, cf. Comptes rendus).

Riemann, by contrast, has assigned the scope ('amplitudinem') of the conditions necessary for determining the function. The next page adds that the usual definitions seem to contain superfluous characteristics ('notae superfluae').

Mathematical content, in modern terms (my gloss):
- Thesis I: w is a function of z iff dw/dz is independent of the direction of dz, i.e. the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x hold. This replaces definition by analytic expression.
- Thesis III: a function is determined by boundary and discontinuity data (Dirichlet-principle uniqueness, dissertation §§18-20). Determination by a formula is not part of the definition.
- The theorem in II is plausibly a dissertation statement such as the removable-singularity type theorem (§12). This is uncertain.
errors: No mathematical steps on the page; nothing to check for correctness.

The page references (pag. 16, art. 4/12) are drafts and may not match the printed dissertation's pagination; the quoted words 'welche allgemein zu reden' do not obviously match the famous §1 definition, so the reference is uncertain.

results.what: Defining a complex function by the condition that dw/dz is independent of the direction of dz, rather than by an analytic expression, stated as a disputation thesis against prevailing views (Cauchy).
results.modern_name: Holomorphic function via Cauchy-Riemann equations (complex differentiability as definition)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (dissertation); Cauchy and d'Alembert/Euler for the equations; Cauchy's 'monogène' 1851

results.what: Claim that a function is determined by necessary conditions (boundary values and discontinuities), not by an analytic expression.
results.modern_name: Riemann's existence/uniqueness approach (Dirichlet principle) to determining analytic functions

results.what: Draft list of disputation theses positioned polemically against Cauchy.

deep.surprise_reason: The content restates known positions of Riemann's 1851 dissertation. The only mildly interesting detail is the explicit framing of the disputation theses as points of disagreement with Cauchy (Comptes rendus).

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); u=re(expand((x+I*y)**3)); v=im(expand((x+I*y)**3)); simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y))==0 and simplify(diff(u,y)+diff(v,x))==0
checkable.asserts: w=z^3 satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations, i.e. is a 'function of z' in Riemann's definitional sense.
w = conj(z) fails Riemann's definition (dw/dz depends on the direction of dz), though it is given by an analytic expression in x and y.

transcription_corrections: Line 2 of thesis II reference likely reads 'pag. 16. art. 12' (or 'art. 4'), not 'cet. 4'; red marks are in the image there.
'ratione' (in red ink, left margin) belongs with 'polemica ratione non scripsimus'.
'eo omnes valent' is uncertain; the sense is 'in eo conveniunt / commune habent, ut ab expressione analytica proficiscantur'.
'Ab hac re Hanc' is likely 'Ab hac re Hanc [ipsam] notionem', i.e. 'this same notion', with 'eandem' interlinear.
